raw_case_text: A 32-year-old male with HIV presented with a 1-month history of pruritic erythematous scaly patches on the scrotum, groin, and thighs, progressing to painful pustules and erosions in the preceding 4 days. The patient was 174 cm in height and weighed 68 kg. Previous mycological examinations of the scrotum and inguinal regions, conducted at multiple healthcare facilities, consistently yielded negative results. History revealed routine use of "Huoli 28 Disinfectant" (containing benzalkonium chloride) for soaking flat-angle underwear due to HIV-related hygiene practices. Laboratory investigations revealed an HIV viral load below the lower limit of quantification (<1.0E+2 IU/mL). The patient is currently maintained on oral lopinavir/ritonavir and zidovudine/lamivudine combination therapy.Initial misdiagnosis as eczema showed partial response to corticosteroids but rebounded severely upon discontinuation. Dermatological examination revealed symmetrically distributed dull-red patches, erosions, and pustules involving the scrotum, inguinal regions, and thighs (Figure 1a). A close-up view of the eruption on the right thigh is shown in Figure 1b. Histopathology of thigh lesions revealed hyperkeratosis, granular parakeratosis, granular basophilic keratohyalin granules, intra-corneal pustules, and mild dermal lymphocytic infiltration (Figure 2a). Dermoscopy of the thigh revealed a faint reddish background with relatively uniform dotted and globular vessels, accompanied by mild scaling (Figure 2b). Mycological examination of the scrotum and inguinal region was negative, while direct microscopy of the thigh lesion was positive for fungal elements; culture subsequently identified Candida albicans (Figure 2c). Concurrent CD4+ lymphopenia was observed (CD4+ count: 320 cells/muL; CD4+/CD8+ ratio: 0.58). The present case exhibited the following features: prior exposure to benzalkonium chloride, involvement of intertriginous areas, peripheral parchment-like desquamation, histopathological findings of keratohyalin granules within the stratum corneum, and Candida species isolation on fungal culture. Based on these collective findings, the patient was diagnosed with GP with concomitant candidiasis. Tinea corporis and tinea cruris are common dermatoses in people living with HIV and were therefore key differential diagnoses in this case. The patient was not diagnosed solely with these conditions for the following reasons: repeated mycological examinations of the scrotum and inguinal regions:conducted at multiple hospitals including our institution:were negative; Candida species were only isolated from a culture of the thigh lesion during the current presentation. Notably, the most severely affected area was the medial thigh, a site consistently in close contact with the patient's boxer shorts, which likely led to increased and prolonged exposure to benzalkonium chloride residues. The medial thigh, subjected to the most intense and prolonged exposure to benzalkonium chloride, consequently sustained the greatest compromise to its skin barrier function. This local vulnerability, compounded by the systemic immunosuppression associated with HIV infection, created a permissive environment for secondary candidal infection at this specific site.The cutaneous lesions resolved completely following an 8-day course of intravenous compound glycyrrhizin (60 mL once daily) combined with cessation of benzalkonium chloride exposure.The healing process was documented with serial clinical photographs capturing the daily progression of the cutaneous lesions from days 1 to 8 (Figure 3a-h), along with the follow-up assessment on day 27 (Figure 3i). To allow for more detailed observation, close-up views of the right thigh were obtained, documenting the daily evolution of the skin lesions from days 1 to 8 post-treatment (Figure 4a-h), as well as the follow-up assessment on day 27 (Figure 4i). Notably, on day 2, after fungal microscopy returned positive, topical naphthifine and ketoconazole cream was applied but subsequently discontinued due to reported stinging sensation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old HIV-positive male presented with a 1-month history of pruritic erythematous scaly patches on the scrotum, groin, and thighs that progressed over the preceding 4 days to painful pustules and erosions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One month prior to presentation, the patient developed pruritic erythematous scaly plaques in his scrotal, inguinal, and thigh regions. He had been misdiagnosed at outside clinics with eczema (with transient partial response to topical corticosteroids followed by severe rebound upon discontinuation) and had multiple negative outside mycological smears of the groin and scrotum. Four days prior to presentation, the lesions progressed to painful pustules and erosions. History revealed routine soaking of his boxer-brief underwear in 'Huoli 28 Disinfectant' containing benzalkonium chloride.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of HIV infection stably maintained on combination antiretroviral therapy; routine exposure of underwear to benzalkonium chloride disinfectant.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for inguinal/scrotal/thigh pruritus, pain, pustules, and erosions. Home medications: oral lopinavir/ritonavir and zidovudine/lamivudine. Experienced local stinging upon application of topical napftifine-ketoconazole cream.

objective.physical_examination: Height 174 cm, weight 68 kg. Dermatological examination revealed symmetrically distributed dull-red erythematous patches, peripheral parchment-like desquamation, erosions, and pustules involving the scrotum, bilateral inguinal folds, and medial thighs (most severe on the medial thighs contacting his underwear).
objective.routine_investigations: Direct potassium hydroxide microscopy and fungal culture of the scrotum and inguinal folds were negative, whereas direct fungal microscopy of the medial thigh lesion was positive for fungal elements and culture isolated Candida albicans.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-lymphocyte count was 320 cells/µL with a CD4+/CD8+ ratio of 0.58. Dermoscopy of the right thigh lesion showed a faint reddish background with uniform dotted and globular vessels and mild scaling. Skin biopsy histopathology of the thigh lesion demonstrated hyperkeratosis, granular parakeratosis with retained basophilic keratohyalin granules in the stratum corneum, intracorneal pustules, and mild dermal lymphocytic infiltration.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Benzalkonium chloride-induced granular parakeratosis (GP) complicated by secondary cutaneous Candida albicans infection in a 32-year-old male with virologically suppressed HIV infection (plasma HIV viral load <1.0 x 10^2 IU/mL, CD4+ count 320 cells/µL, CD4/CD8 ratio 0.58 on lopinavir/ritonavir and zidovudine/lamivudine). Primary tinea cruris/corporis was excluded by repeatedly negative dermatophyte microscopy and cultures, while GP was confirmed by benzalkonium chloride exposure history and pathognomonic retained stratum corneum basophilic keratohyalin granules on histopathology. Topical napftifine-ketoconazole cream was discontinued on day 2 due to local stinging; the patient was treated with immediate cessation of benzalkonium chloride disinfectant exposure and an 8-day course of intravenous compound glycyrrhizin (60 mL once daily), achieving complete resolution of all cutaneous lesions by day 8 and sustained clearance at day 27 follow-up.
